description: ¡Hola! Somos SpacePlants Lab, enfocado en diseñar una planta capaz de adaptarse al entorno lunar. Nuestro proyecto combina ciencia, creatividad, diseño de misiones espaciales y realidad virtual para explorar nuevas posibilidades de vida más allá de la Tierra.
summary:
SpacePlants Lab is a web-based mission design game. Players design and run a space greenhouse inspired by NASA’s Veggie and Advanced Plant Habitat systems on the International Space Station. First they pick a crop: romaine lettuce, mizuna, kale, radish or chile pepper. Then they build the growth chamber from real components such as LED lights, wick watering, pumps, electrovalves and sensors, while staying within a 22 kg mass limit and a power budget. Once the mission starts, a simulation tracks five vital variables: light, water, substrate moisture, temperature and oxygen. These change with a 16/8 photoperiod and random events. Players can only correct them by winning short, space-themed minigames featuring NASA spacecraft, astronauts and scientists, the planets and Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena. The goal is to reach harvest day with a healthy plant.

The problem: growing food in space is key to long missions to the Moon and Mars, but most students never get to see how hard it is to keep a plant alive in microgravity. SpacePlants Lab turns that engineering challenge into a playable experience. It teaches resource management, systems thinking and space history, and it runs in English and Spanish in any browser with nothing to install.
details:
What exactly does it do?

SpacePlants Lab simulates a full space-farming mission, from design to harvest. The player acts as a mission engineer who has to:

  • Choose a crop that NASA has grown or studied for space (romaine lettuce, mizuna, kale, radish or chile pepper), each with its own growth time, moisture, temperature, light needs and sensitivity.
  • Design the growth chamber by choosing components in nine categories (watering, lighting, sensors, air control, thermal protection, power and more). Each component has a real mass in kg and power in W, and the design must stay under a 22 kg launch limit.
  • Get a mission evaluation (Easy, Medium or Hard) that explains which choices were good and which were risky.
  • Run a simulation where every in-game day lasts 3 real minutes, with speed controls from x0.5 to x5.
  • Protect the plant by winning minigames, the only way to restore the five variables:
    • Water reservoir → spacecraft sliding puzzle (Voyager 1, Apollo 11, Discovery, New Horizons, Orion)
    • Substrate moisture → memory game with NASA pioneers from three generations
    • Temperature → tile-swap puzzle of places in the Solar System (Sun, Venus, Moon, Mars, Europa)
    • Oxygen → "Whack-the-Alien" reflex game inspired by NASA's UAP study
    • LED power (light) → tic-tac-toe against a strategic AI
  • Harvest the plant inside the harvest window, or lose it if the variables stay critical too long. Best results are saved as records.

How does it work?

  1. Crop selection: the player picks one of five crops. Each crop sets the simulation's parameters: cycle length, ideal moisture and temperature ranges, light intensity (PAR), water use and stress sensitivity.
  2. Chamber design: the player picks one component per category. The game adds up mass (max 22 kg) and power use and shows real information about each component on hover.
  3. Mission evaluation: a rules engine reviews the design. Good choices (for example the absorbent wick, the same system used by NASA's Veggie) lower the difficulty, and risky ones raise it.
  4. Growth simulation: a crop model updates five variables in real time. Light follows a 16-hour on / 8-hour off photoperiod and drains the LED battery. Water and substrate moisture depend on the chosen watering system. Temperature and oxygen drift and react to random events such as leaks or thermal failures. When a variable leaves its safe range the plant takes damage, and when it comes back the plant recovers. The plant is drawn procedurally and grows, droops or wilts depending on its health.
  5. Minigames: clicking "Recharge" on a variable opens its minigame. Winning restores the variable, a tie gives a partial recharge, and the player can leave at any time with no penalty. Each minigame includes an info panel about the real spacecraft, scientist or place shown.
  6. Harvest: when the growth cycle ends, the harvest window opens. A healthy harvest completes the mission and shows a report with time in range, events and a management grade.

What benefits does it have?

Educational: it teaches how plants are grown in space using real NASA systems (Veggie, Advanced Plant Habitat) and real limits like mass, power and photoperiod. Every design choice affects the simulation that follows, which builds systems thinking. Players also learn space history through real spacecraft, astronauts and scientists.

Social: the game is bilingual (English and Spanish), so Spanish-speaking students in Latin America can use it. It is free and runs in any browser with no installation or account, so it works on low-cost school computers. Sessions are short and replayable, which fits classrooms and science fairs.

Economic: it is open source and hosted for free on GitHub Pages, so schools and teachers can use and adapt it without paying licenses. It also raises awareness of controlled-environment agriculture, which matters for food security on Earth too (vertical farms, harsh climates).

What do you hope to achieve?

Short term: get students in Arequipa, Peru, and other Spanish-speaking communities playing a space mission design game in their own language, present it at schools and outreach events, and use player feedback to balance difficulty.

Long term: add more NASA crops and Moon or Mars habitat scenarios, create a teacher mode with lesson guides and data export, and help inspire a new generation of Latin American scientists and engineers to take part in space exploration.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Game engine and programming: Godot Engine 4.7.2, GDScript
  • Web: HTML5 / WebAssembly (Godot Web export); HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the presentation
  • Version control and deployment: Git, GitHub, GitHub Desktop, GitHub Pages
  • Testing: Godot automated test scripts; Python + Playwright with Google Chrome
  • Design and content: procedural drawing in Godot, Google Fonts, NASA Image and Video Library
  • Artificial intelligence: Claude (Anthropic)
  • Hardware: personal laptops; the game runs in standard desktop web browsers

Plus: workflows

Mission Workflow: the steps a player goes through, the resource management loop and what happens when variables go out of range.

Team Workflow: how our team split the work across biotechnology, mechatronics, game development and content, from research to deployment.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Our team used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant for:

  • Programming: help writing and organizing the GDScript code (crop simulation model, minigames, interface and bilingual translation system).
  • Debugging and testing: finding and fixing errors and writing automated test scripts.
  • Research: summarizing public NASA information about Veggie, the Advanced Plant Habitat and ISS crops. We checked everything against the NASA sources listed in this submission.
  • Writing and translation: in-game text, the presentation and this report (Spanish ↔ English).
  • Visual design: procedural illustrations, the web presentation and the workflow diagrams. AI-assisted diagrams are labeled as such.

The team made every design decision, chose the game mechanics and reviewed and tested all of the final content.
